query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled low-temperature annealing following a moderate pre-strain will induce interfacial recrystallization and fine nano‐precipitation along the lamellar colony boundaries of the eutectic high-entropy alloy, thereby reducing dislocation pile-ups and mitigating local stress concentrations that lead to microcracking and brittleness.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colonies that display dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries, resulting in limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness.
generation.intervention: Low-temperature annealing after a controlled, moderate pre-deformation (pre-strain) treatment.
generation.conditions: The treatment is applied at a sub-transus temperature under controlled conditions following a moderate amount of pre-strain, prior to room-temperature tensile testing under standard quasi-static loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A modified internal boundary structure featuring interfacial recrystallization and fine nano‐precipitates along colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The intervention relaxes internal stress concentrations by promoting recrystallization at the boundaries and generating nano-precipitates that act as obstacles to dislocation pile-up, thereby reducing microcrack initiation while maintaining or enhancing intrinsic strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to exhibit increased ductility along with retained or improved tensile strength compared to the untreated material because of the reduced likelihood of catastrophic microcracking from dislocation pile-ups.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy, which shows brittleness and limited ductility due to stress concentration from dislocation accumulation at internal colony boundaries during straining.
generation.boundary: These improvements are anticipated to be valid under standard room-temperature tensile conditions; however, the benefits might diminish if the loading conditions significantly deviate from quasi-static tension or if the pre-strain and annealing parameters are not precisely optimized.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvements in tensile ductility and strength is uncertain and will depend on the precise control of the pre-strain level, annealing temperature, and duration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same eutectic high-entropy alloy batch. One set undergoes the proposed moderate pre-strain followed by low-temperature annealing under the prescribed conditions, while the other set remains untreated. Conduct room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests under identical quasi-static loading conditions and compare the mechanical properties and microstructural features.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (using TEM/SEM to assess boundary recrystallization and nano‐precipitate formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically treated specimens do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in elongation (i.e., ductility) while maintaining or increasing tensile strength relative to the untreated specimens, or if microcracking due to dislocation pile-ups is still prevalent, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
